item.text: {"text":"[HSTU (ICML 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) establishes the sequential-transduction backbone, but does not itself establish that history sensitivity identifies recent intent. Stronger diagnostic precedents come from [Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://github.com/Antondfger/Does-It-Look-Sequential/): compare original versus shuffled histories using a frozen model, measure HR@10/NDCG@10 and recommendation overlap, and bootstrap user-level differences. Effects vary substantially across datasets. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) explicitly distinguishes excessive recent-item emphasis from useful long-term preference modeling. [Counterfactual explanations via genetic algorithms (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal history edits that change recommendations; these explain model behavior rather than establish causal effects on users.\n\nSuggested HSTU adaptation: pair each original history with suffix truncation, prefix-only shuffling that preserves the latest event, recent-event removal versus equally sized older-event removal, and irrelevant-event insertion matched on training frequency and insertion position. Define irrelevance operationally using available titles/descriptions; it is not observed user intent. Keep candidates fixed, preserve left padding and final-nonpadding readout, and track target-score changes, positive–negative margin changes, rank changes, and HR@10. Bootstrap users within category, then macro-average category effects. Within the same trained model, compare perturbation-induced representation changes by HSTU layer and temporarily bypass individual residual updates; treat bypass results cautiously because they introduce distribution shift. Larger effects from recent removal than matched older removal suggest recency dependence; additional effects from prefix shuffling suggest order dependence. These are proposed diagnostic controls, not established HSTU-specific findings, and sensitivity alone is not causal evidence."}
